theme: My heart overflows, the royal wedding
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 45. This is a royal wedding song. Read it as a song for a king and his bride, and then read it again with the Messiah in mind.
settingTheScene: The title calls it “A Maskil of the Sons of Korah, a love song,” set to the tune “Lilies.” It was probably composed for a royal wedding in Israel, perhaps even Solomon’s. After the story of Solomon’s accession, it is a fitting psalm to hear. But the language is so lofty that it was early read as pointing to the Messiah, and the New Testament quotes it that way.
observation: “My heart overflows with a pleasing theme; I address my verses to the king; my tongue is like the pen of a ready scribe” (v. 1).
“You are the most handsome of the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever” (v. 2).
“In your majesty ride out victoriously for the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness” (v. 4).
“Your throne, O God, is forever and ever. The scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of uprightness” (v. 6).
“You love righteousness and hate wickedness. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions” (v. 7).
“At your right hand stands the queen in gold of Ophir” (v. 9).
“Hear, O daughter, consider, and incline your ear: forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty” (vv. 10-11).
“I will cause your name to be remembered in all generations; therefore nations will praise you forever and ever” (v. 17).
interpretation:
The psalm is a love song, and it shows that the Bible is not embarrassed by joy at a wedding. The poet describes the king in glowing terms: handsome, gracious in speech, a warrior who rides out “for the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness.” The three words are unexpected for a king. A king who fights for truth, for meekness (humility), and righteousness is no ordinary monarch.

Then comes the surprise. The poet turns and addresses the king: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.” In the Hebrew, the king is addressed as “God.” Some readers have understood it as a figure of speech for the king’s godlike authority, but the line goes beyond the limits of any mere human king. The psalm raises a question that only the New Testament answers: who is this king whose throne is eternal and who is addressed as God?

The king is anointed “with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.” It is an echo of the Messiah’s anointing. And the king has a bride. In the second half of the psalm, the queen is told to forget her father’s house and to honor the king. She is given beautiful garments and brought in with joy. The picture of a royal marriage became, for the prophets and then the apostles, a picture of God’s covenant with his people.

The psalm ends with a promise that the king’s name will be remembered forever and that the nations will praise him. It is a promise that no human wedding could fulfill, but one that looks beyond to a king whose reign has no end.

Read in its original setting, it celebrates the royal house of David. Read in light of the whole Bible, it points to the wedding of the Lamb.
connection: Hebrews 1:8-9 quotes verses 6 and 7 and applies them directly to the Son: “But of the Son he says, Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.” The psalm is a witness to Christ’s deity. Paul describes the church as Christ’s bride (Ephesians 5:25-32), and Revelation 19:7-9 and 21:2 describe the marriage supper of the Lamb. John 3:29 says, “The one who has the bride is the bridegroom.”
application:
Read verses 6 and 7 aloud as praise to Jesus, whom Hebrews says is addressed here.

Think about how your relationship with Christ is like that of a bride with her husband.

Pray for the church, that she would be ready for the wedding.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what fills your heart when you think of Christ, the King.
Thank him that the King loves his bride, the church.
Ask him to make you faithful to the King.
